phrases.phrase: On May 11th, thirty-nine gems appeared in the Ruby registry. A rehearsal. Nobody noticed.
The next day: 516 more in under fourteen hours — 271 in a single hour. The registry was flooding.

Inside each gem: a go-import tag dressed as a hijack — aimed at council calendars through a reader proxy, cycling git, hg, fossil, bzr, svn. But the address it claimed was the registry's own API. No real go get could fire it. The tags were canaries — proof the ghosts could inject raw HTML into the registry at scale. The code did nothing: x=1. One gem even signed it: southwarkssrfhack.

But thirty-nine gems carried builders: steal a council calendar page — certificate checks off — forge a brand-new gem from it, and push it straight back into RubyGems, using API keys hardcoded inside the gems themselves. Fifty-four carried full push credentials. It wasn't probing the registry. It was living in it.

One gem flipped innocent to weaponized between versions. A captured log shows their own rig blocked by a network filter. An internal timestamp — 02:17:55 UTC — confirms the burst from the inside. And the keys rotated: the leaked ones were just bootstrap. Revoking them wouldn't have stopped it.
RubyGems yanked the gems, halted registrations, disclosed a cache bug. In June, a smaller wave tried plain link-posting at a US federal dataset. Same ghosts, simpler trick.
Then July 7th: JFrog found it was bigger. Three thousand twenty-two packages — a third mechanism family: webhook dead drops in the woods, marked A000 and ZZEND.
The registry was haunted long before anyone looked.
